content: Drug-drug interactions must be carefully considered when using antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and direct-acting antiviral agents for hepatitis C (HCV) infection. Ledipasvir and velpatasvir, when combined with sofosbuvir, exhibit a reduced potential for interactions with ARV drugs due to their use of different metabolic pathways. Regimens containing grazoprevir or glecaprevir are contraindicated with atazanavir (ATV) and darunavir (DRV). Direct-acting antiviral agents for HCV do not interact with other nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) or unboosted integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs). For opioid substitution therapy, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends methadone or buprenorphine for opioid dependence. Co-administration of efavirenz (EFV) reduces methadone and buprenorphine concentrations, potentially causing withdrawal symptoms and increasing the risk of opioid relapse. Patients on methadone and EFV should be closely monitored, and methadone doses may need adjustment if withdrawal symptoms occur. Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) may also reduce methadone concentrations, and both drugs are associated with QT prolongation. Mental health medications require careful management when co-administered with ARV drugs due to potential drug-drug interactions. Quetiapine should only be used with PIs if absolutely necessary, and at one-sixth of the normal dose. Enzyme-inducing non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) like EFV and nevirapine (NVP) may decrease quetiapine levels, risking suboptimal effects. Pimozide is contraindicated with PIs due to the risk of serious or life-threatening reactions, such as cardiac arrhythmias. Many mental health medications, including lithium, haloperidol, and fluphenazine, can prolong the QT interval, requiring caution when combined with PIs. No pharmacokinetic interactions occur with NRTIs or unboosted INSTIs. Hormonal contraceptives and high-dose hormonal therapy for gender-affirming care may have altered steroid hormone levels when used with ARV drugs. EFV can reduce the efficacy of contraceptives, including implants, vaginal rings, and transdermal contraceptives, necessitating the use of reliable barrier methods to prevent unintended pregnancy. For emergency contraception in women taking EFV, a copper intrauterine device is preferred, or alternatively, a single dose of 3 mg levonorgestrel can be used. Injectable formulations of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) are unaffected by ARV drugs and can be used without restrictions. WHO provides recommendations on hormonal contraceptive use in women receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). High-dose hormonal therapy for gender transitioning does not affect ARV drug efficacy. Dolutegravir (DTG), raltegravir (RAL), newer NNRTIs, and NRTIs do not interact with gender-affirming hormones, but hormone doses may need adjustment when used with PIs, EFV, or NVP. Dosage recommendations for gender-affirming hormone therapy are available in prescribing resources, such as the HIV drug interaction website of the University of Liverpool. Protease inhibitors (PIs) increase the concentrations of the antihypertensive drug amlodipine, warranting a 50% dose reduction. Dosage adjustments may also be necessary for antidiabetic drugs like glibenclamide and gliclazide when used with PIs. High doses of metformin should be avoided, and close monitoring is recommended for individuals with moderate renal impairment. WHO recommends statins for individuals with a 10-year cardiovascular risk exceeding 30%. Boosted PIs are contraindicated with simvastatin due to the risk of rhabdomyolysis. Atorvastatin can be used with PIs, but the daily dose should be limited to 10 mg with ATV/r, 40 mg with DRV/r, and 20 mg with LPV/r. Dose increases may be needed with EFV and NVP. Statins do not interact with DTG, RAL, or NRTIs. Dexamethasone, used in doses ranging from 6 mg to 20 mg daily for short durations in COVID-19 patients, has a weak to moderate inducing effect that does not require dose adjustments of EFV, NVP, PIs, DTG, or RAL. However, EFV and NVP may decrease dexamethasone concentrations, and doubling the dexamethasone dose is recommended. No drug-drug interactions are expected between ARV drugs and COVID-19 vaccines. DTG should not be administered simultaneously with cation-containing antacids, laxatives, or multivitamin/mineral supplements due to the risk of chelation. If combined, DTG should be taken two hours before or six hours after medications containing polyvalent cations.
